newsitem.title: USA: Spy Factory and owner handed stiff sentences.
newsitem.headline: Spy Factory and owner handed stiff sentences.

text.p: The Spy Factory, the nation's largest chain of "spy shops," and its owner were sentenced on charges involving smuggling and selling illegal bugging and wiretapping devices, federal prosecutors said Thursday.

The company's owner, Ronald Kimball, was sentenced to four years and three months in prison and was ordered by U.S. District Judge Sonia Sotomayor to forfeit $2.3 million, which represents the proceeds from Spy Factory's illegal sales of wiretapping and bugging devices.
The sentences were handed out late Wednesday.
The San Antonio-based chain was shut down in March shortly after a plea hearing in Manhattan federal court at which the judge ordered Spy Factory and all of its assets forfeited to the United States.

The judge also ordered Kimball, a former federal Drug Enforcement Administration agent who founded Spy Factory, barred from working in any similar business during his three-year probation after his release.

Also sentenced was Tracy Edward Ford, the former deputy general manager who was given six months of home confinement and three years probation. He was also barred from engaging in the sale of electronic devices during his probation.
Marlin Richardson, the company's former general manager, will be sentenced next month.

Spy Factory, its owner and executives pleaded guilty in March to 69 counts of money laundering, smuggling, selling illegal wiretapping and bugging devices and conspiracy between 1989 and 1995 after a one-week trial.
At the time of the 1995 indictment, the Spy Factory had stores in Arizona, California, Colorado, Georgia, Illinois, Missouri, Nevada, Texas, Utah and Washington.

The defendants were indicted in August 1995 on charges that they bought devices from the Japanese firm Micro Electronics Ind. Co. of Tokyo, which prosecutors allege is the largest international supplier of illegal bugging and wiretapping devices.
